description: Precision AgriTech - Agronomic Advisory Knowledge Base. Covers all 12 target crop-disease classes defined in Phase 1. Indexed by PlantVillage class labels.

Tomato___healthy.general_description: The tomato plant shows no signs of disease, pest damage, or nutritional deficiency. Foliage displays uniform deep green coloration with firm, turgid leaf tissue. Continue standard agronomic practice.
cultural_controls: Maintain adequate plant spacing (45–60 cm) to promote airflow and reduce humidity.
Monitor soil moisture and maintain consistent irrigation to avoid drought stress.
Rotate crops annually to prevent soilborne disease buildup.
Inspect plants weekly for early signs of pest or pathogen activity.
Tomato___healthy.immediate_action: No intervention required. Continue routine field monitoring and maintain preventative spray calendar.

Tomato___Early_blight.general_description: Early Blight is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. Characteristic concentric brown lesions with a target-like pattern appear on older, lower leaves first, progressing upward. Severe infections cause premature defoliation, reducing photosynthetic capacity and yield by 20–30%.
Tomato___Early_blight.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (24–29°C), high relative humidity (>80%), extended leaf wetness (>6 hours), and alternating wet-dry cycles. Nitrogen-deficient plants are significantly more susceptible.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply every 7–10 days beginning at first sign of disease or during high-risk weather windows.
Apply preventatively before rain events or when humidity exceeds 80% for >6 hours.
Apply at first symptom appearance; do not exceed 3 applications per season to prevent resistance.
Apply as a protective spray every 10–14 days in humid conditions.

cultural_controls: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves immediately to reduce inoculum load.
Avoid overhead irrigation; switch to drip or furrow irrigation to minimize leaf wetness duration.
Apply nitrogen fertilization as split doses to maintain adequate plant nutrition and resistance.
Implement minimum 3-year crop rotation with non-Solanaceous crops.
Use certified disease-free transplants and resistant cultivars (e.g., Plum Regal, Mountain Magic).
Mulch the soil surface to prevent rain splash dispersal of soilborne conidia.

biological_controls.notes: Preventative mode of action; most effective when applied before disease onset.
Suppresses soilborne inoculum; combine with copper-based foliar sprays for integrated management.

Tomato___Early_blight.immediate_action: Remove all visibly infected lower leaves. Switch to drip irrigation immediately. Apply Mancozeb 80% WP or Chlorothalonil as a protective spray. Monitor daily for disease progression.

Tomato___Late_blight.general_description: Late Blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans — the same pathogen responsible for the Irish Potato Famine of 1845. Water-soaked, dark olive-green to brown lesions rapidly expand across leaves, stems, and fruits. A characteristic white cottony sporulation (sporangiophores) appears on the underside of infected tissue in humid conditions. Under favorable weather, entire crops can be destroyed within 1–2 weeks without intervention.
Tomato___Late_blight.favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (15–22°C), relative humidity >90%, extended leaf wetness (>10 hours), rain events followed by cool nights. Particularly severe in coastal and valley regions with persistent morning fog.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at first symptom appearance; repeat every 5–7 days under high disease pressure.
Apply within 24–48 hours of infection event; highly systemic.
Apply preventatively or immediately after a high-risk weather event.
Apply every 5–7 days as a protective barrier during high-risk periods.

cultural_controls: IMMEDIATELY isolate affected parcels — do not allow workers or equipment to pass through infected areas without decontamination.
Destroy all infected plant material by deep burial or incineration (do NOT compost).
Eliminate overhead irrigation; switch to drip irrigation only to eliminate foliar wetness.
Implement strict crop rotation — do not plant Solanaceous crops on affected land for 3+ years.
Monitor neighboring fields and report confirmed outbreaks to local agricultural authority.
Apply stramineous mulch to suppress soilborne sporangia splash-dispersal.
Plant certified blight-resistant cultivars (e.g., Defiant PhR, Mountain Merit).

biological_controls.notes: Preventative only; not effective on established infections. Use as part of an integrated spray program with copper-based fungicides.

Tomato___Late_blight.immediate_action: CRITICAL: Isolate affected perimeter immediately. Restrict all overhead irrigation. Apply a curative fungicide (Cymoxanil + Mancozeb or Dimethomorph) within 24 hours. Notify neighboring farm operators. Prepare contingency harvest of unaffected fruit if disease spread exceeds 30% canopy coverage.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.general_description: Bacterial Spot is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria. Symptoms include small, water-soaked, angular lesions on leaves that turn dark brown with yellow halos. On fruit, sunken, dark, scab-like lesions reduce marketability. The disease spreads rapidly by rain splash and aerosols in warm, wet conditions.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (24–30°C), high relative humidity (>80%), rain events, overhead irrigation, and high nitrogen nutrition. Bacteria can survive in seed and crop debris.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Begin applications at transplanting; repeat every 7 days during wet periods.
Apply preventatively before rain events; do not apply when temperatures exceed 32°C to avoid phytotoxicity.
Apply at first symptom or after each rain event above 10 mm.

cultural_controls: Use certified pathogen-free seed; treat seed with hot water (50°C for 25 minutes) before planting.
Eliminate overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation to minimize leaf wetness.
Remove and dispose of infected plant debris at season end; do not leave in field.
Disinfect pruning tools between plants with 10% bleach solution or 70% isopropyl alcohol.
Maintain adequate plant spacing to reduce canopy humidity.
Plant resistant or tolerant cultivars where available.

biological_controls.notes: Apply as a preventative at 7–10 day intervals; may be tank-mixed with copper bactericides.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.immediate_action: Stop overhead irrigation immediately. Apply copper-based bactericide within 48 hours. Remove and destroy all heavily infected tissue. Disinfect all field equipment before movement to adjacent parcels.

Potato___healthy.general_description: The potato plant is in healthy condition with no visible signs of foliar disease, pest activity, or nutritional stress. Continue standard management practices.
cultural_controls: Use certified disease-free seed tubers from trusted suppliers.
Maintain adequate hilling to protect developing tubers from greening and late blight.
Monitor soil moisture to avoid waterlogging, which predisposes plants to Pythium and bacterial rot.
Scout fields weekly for early signs of aphid colonies (vectors of Potato Virus Y and PVX).
Potato___healthy.immediate_action: No intervention required. Maintain preventative spray schedule based on Blight Forecasting models (e.g., BLITECAST) or regional disease alert systems.

Potato___Early_blight.general_description: Potato Early Blight, caused by Alternaria solani, produces characteristic target-like concentric ring lesions on older lower leaves. Unlike Late Blight, lesions are dry and angular, often surrounded by a yellow chlorotic halo. The disease progresses upward as the season advances and accelerates under warm, humid conditions.
Potato___Early_blight.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (24–29°C), high relative humidity (>80%), periods of dry weather alternating with rain, and nutrient-stressed plants (particularly nitrogen and potassium deficiency).

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply every 10–14 days starting at row closure (canopy closure).
Apply as a protective spray before expected rain events.
Apply at first symptom appearance; maximum 3 applications per season.

cultural_controls: Apply balanced NPK fertilization — adequate nitrogen and potassium significantly reduce susceptibility.
Remove heavily infected haulm tissue; do not leave in field after harvest.
Implement 3–4 year crop rotation with cereals or legumes.
Use certified seed tubers with known disease resistance.
Avoid overhead irrigation during evening hours to reduce nocturnal leaf wetness.

biological_controls.notes: Best applied preventatively at 7-day intervals; can be combined with conventional fungicide programs.

Potato___Early_blight.immediate_action: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves. Apply Mancozeb 80% WP or Chlorothalonil protectively. Ensure adequate potassium and nitrogen nutrition via leaf tissue test.

Potato___Late_blight.general_description: Potato Late Blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, is the most destructive potato disease worldwide. Pale green to brown water-soaked lesions appear on leaves and rapidly expand; white sporulation is visible on the underside of leaves in moist conditions. Infected stems collapse, and tubers develop brown, granular internal rot (storage rot). A single infected field can be completely destroyed within 7–10 days under epidemic conditions.
Potato___Late_blight.favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (10–20°C), prolonged relative humidity >90%, rain events, fog, and extended periods of leaf wetness (>10 hours). The pathogen survives in volunteer potato plants and infected tubers in storage or soil.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at first sign of disease or after a Blitecast warning threshold is exceeded; repeat every 7–14 days.
Apply preventatively or at very early infection; most effective before symptom expression.
Apply every 5–7 days during high-risk weather windows.

cultural_controls: IMMEDIATELY destroy or desiccate infected haulm (diquat or mechanical destruction) to prevent tuber infection.
Delay harvest by 2–3 weeks after haulm destruction to allow tuber skin set and reduce storage rot.
Never store or replant tubers from a blight-affected field.
Eliminate all volunteer potato plants in and around the field.
Implement a rigorous 4–5 year rotation; never plant potatoes after tomatoes.
Plant certified blight-resistant cultivars (e.g., Sarpo Mira, Penta, Innovator).

biological_controls.notes: Preventative use only as part of an integrated blight management program; pair with copper-based protectants.

Potato___Late_blight.immediate_action: CRITICAL: Begin haulm desiccation protocol on severely affected parcels immediately. Apply a systemic curative fungicide (Metalaxyl-M + Mancozeb) within 24 hours. Cease all irrigation. Alert neighboring potato growers. Check tuber lots in storage for early rot symptoms.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.general_description: The corn (maize) plant is in healthy condition with vibrant green foliage and no evidence of disease lesions, rust pustules, or foliar blight symptoms. Maintain current crop management practice.
cultural_controls: Monitor for European corn borer and western corn rootworm populations during silking.
Maintain adequate side-dress nitrogen applications at V6 growth stage.
Ensure adequate plant population density (70,000–90,000 plants/ha) for targeted hybrid.
Scout bi-weekly for early disease signs, particularly in late July/August when conditions favor rust and blight.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.immediate_action: No intervention required. Maintain preventative scouting program and weather-based disease monitoring.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.general_description: Common Rust, caused by Puccinia sorghi, is an obligate biotrophic fungus producing brick-red to cinnamon-colored urediniospore pustules on both leaf surfaces. Pustules rupture the epidermis and appear in dense clusters along leaf veins. Under severe infection, premature senescence and significant yield losses of 10–30% can occur, particularly in susceptible sweet corn cultivars and late-planted field corn.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (16–23°C), high relative humidity (>95%), extended periods of leaf wetness (dew periods), and cloudy overcast conditions. Urediospores are wind-dispersed over long distances from southern overwintering regions (tropical/subtropical rust nurseries).

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at VT (tasseling) to R2 (blister) growth stage when rust pustules first appear on upper leaves.
Apply from VT through R3 (milk) growth stage; maximum 2 applications per season.
Single application at VT or when rust first detected on ear leaf; highly effective on Puccinia spp.

cultural_controls: Plant rust-resistant hybrids — check seed catalog for Rp gene resistance ratings.
Time planting to avoid peak urediospore dispersal periods in late summer.
Monitor for rust progression from the bottom canopy upward — treatment is most economic at VT stage.
Maintain balanced NPK fertilization; potassium deficiency increases rust susceptibility.

biological_controls.notes: Preventative use; apply at early canopy development before rust season onset.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.immediate_action: Scout the entire field for pustule density. If more than 30% of plants show pustules above the ear leaf at VT stage, apply a triazole or strobilurin-triazole combination fungicide within the next 3–5 days.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.general_description: Northern Leaf Blight (NLB), caused by Exserohilum turcicum, produces distinctive long, elliptical, tan to gray-green lesions (3–15 cm) that run parallel to leaf veins. The lesions have wavy borders and may develop a dark olivaceous sporulation (conidia) under moist conditions. NLB infection above the ear leaf during the grain-fill period (R1–R6) can cause yield losses of 30–50% in highly susceptible hybrids.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (18–27°C), relative humidity >90%, extended periods of leaf wetness (>6 hours), and moderate rainfall. Disease is most severe in areas with minimum tillage and surface corn debris from previous crop.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply at VT (tasseling) through R1 (silking); most critical application window for ear leaf protection.
Apply at VT stage when disease is detected in lower canopy; do not apply after R3 (milk).
Preventative-to-curative application at VT for highly susceptible hybrids in high-disease-risk regions.

cultural_controls: Plant NLB-resistant hybrids — look for Ht1, Ht2, Htm1 gene resistance in seed catalog.
Implement full-inversion plowing or minimum 2-year rotation to decompose infected surface debris.
Avoid planting corn on corn in regions with historically high NLB pressure.
Perform intensive scouting from V10 through R2 to evaluate economic threshold (approximately 50% plants with lesions above ear leaf).
Maintain adequate nitrogen and potassium fertilization to support plant immunity.

biological_controls.notes: Preventative supplemental application during early canopy development; not a replacement for conventional fungicides at VT in high-risk scenarios.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.immediate_action: Evaluate disease severity index (DSI) across the field. If >30% plants show NLB lesions on or above the ear leaf before R3, apply a strobilurin-triazole combination fungicide. Under high-risk conditions, a single well-timed VT application can protect yield potential significantly.

Apple___healthy.general_description: The apple tree foliage is in healthy condition with no visible scab lesions, rust pustules, or foliar disease symptoms. Maintain current integrated pest and disease management schedule.
cultural_controls: Implement a preventative copper fungicide program at green tip and pink bud stages before wet weather.
Prune trees annually during dormancy to improve light penetration and air circulation.
Remove and destroy mummified fruit and fallen leaves — primary inoculum sources for Venturia and Gymnosporangium.
Scout weekly from green tip through petal fall for early disease and pest signs.
Maintain soil pH 6.0–6.5 to optimize nutrient availability and plant health.
Apple___healthy.immediate_action: No intervention required. Maintain scheduled spray program based on apple scab infection model (Mills periods) and regional pathogen pressure alerts.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.general_description: Cedar Apple Rust is a heteroecious rust fungus requiring both apple (or crabapple) and eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) or other susceptible Juniperus species to complete its life cycle. Bright orange-yellow lesions (aecia) appear on the upper surface of apple leaves from petal fall through early summer, often with distinctive tube-like aeciospore horns on the lower leaf surface. Severely infected leaves may drop prematurely, weakening the tree and reducing fruit set in subsequent years.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.favorable_conditions: Wet spring weather with temperatures of 10–24°C during apple bloom and green tip stages. Orange gelatinous telial horns on cedar galls release basidiospores during warm spring rains that infect apple tissue. Orchards within 500 m of susceptible Juniper hosts are at highest risk.

chemical_treatments.application_timing: Apply from silver tip through third cover (5–6 applications); most critical from pink to third cover when spore release peaks.
Apply at pink bud and repeat every 10–14 days through petal fall.
Apply from green tip through first cover as part of a multi-disease protectant program.
Apply at green tip; avoid use when temperatures exceed 32°C to prevent phytotoxicity.

cultural_controls: Remove or eradicate eastern red cedar and susceptible Juniperus hosts within 500 m of the orchard where feasible.
Plant rust-resistant apple cultivars (e.g., Enterprise, Liberty, Freedom, GoldRush).
Prune to improve airflow and reduce canopy humidity during spring infection periods.
Remove infected leaves and mummified fruit at season end to reduce local inoculum.
Monitor regional rust spore release forecasts from local extension services or weather-based models.

biological_controls.notes: Preventative use from green tip through petal fall; pair with sulfur or captan for adequate rust protection in organic systems.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.immediate_action: Apply a triazole fungicide (myclobutanil or tebuconazole) immediately if orange-yellow lesions are detected at or after petal fall. Inspect nearby Juniperus species for active telial horn galls and remove if feasible. Inform neighboring orchard operators of active rust pressure.
